newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian far right calls for rethink on Europe.
newsitem.headline: Austrian far right calls for rethink on Europe.

text.p: Austrian far-right leader Joerg Haider, campaigning before European Union elections, called on Wednesday for a big reduction in contributions to Brussels and a referendum on introduction of a single European currency.

"We are paying too much and getting too little back. The EU is taking too much of our money and ordinary Austrians are digging deep into their pockets," said Haider, whose Freedom Party commands the support of a quarter of Austrian voters.
In a televised debate with leaders from all the main parties in the October 13 vote for the European Parliament, Haider recalled former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.
"We need to be clever about this -- like Britain. They managed to reduce their payments by 30 percent," he said.

Austria, which joined the EU on January 1 last year, contributed 25.6 billion schillings ($2.39 billion) to Brussels in its first year of membership and received 10.1 billion schillings back in subsidies.
"The whole thing was badly negotiated," Haider said, accusing the ruling Social Democrats and conservative People's Party of misleading a trusting Austrian public.

Austria voted to join the EU by a landslide majority in a referendum in June 1994. But Haider claimed the government had reneged on its promise of delivering more jobs after the nation joined the bloc.
"You promised there would be 38,000 more jobs. In fact 30,000 have been lost," he accused Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky.
Austrian unemployment stood at 4.1 percent in August -- among the lowest in Europe but significantly above levels a year ago.
The economic research institute WIFO has forecast another rise in the number of jobless in 1997 as government budget cuts bite deep.
Haider also mounted an attack on EU plans for a single currency. "The people must decide whether we get rid of our schilling," he said.
Vranitzky, who is fighting for his political life in the EU poll, reinforced the government's commitment to European Economic and Monetary Union.
"We say "yes' to monetary union. We say "yes' to the criteria and we say "yes' to the timetable," he said.
A delay could put the whole plan in jeopardy, he added.
The latest opinion polls give the Social Democrats 31 percent support and the People's party 28 percent. Haider's Freedom Party has 25 percent backing.
In a general election in December of last year the Social Democrats won 38 percent of the vote, the People's Party 28 percent and the Freedom Party 22 percent. ($1=10.72 Schilling)
